evals.prompt: I'm in a forecasting hackathon. We submit predictions after the close on day t and get scored on each stock's return from the close of t to the close of t+1. My teammate wrote features.py; sample data is in prices.csv and fundamentals.csv next to it. Can you audit it for look-ahead leakage, fix whatever is wrong, and save a corrected features_fixed.py (same build_features(prices, fundamentals) signature) plus a short audit_report.md that explains each problem and how you checked the fix?
evals.expected_output: Finds all 8 planted leaks, produces a causal features_fixed.py that runs and passes perturbation/truncation tests, and a report.
expectations: Flags prices.dropna(axis=1) as survivorship/look-ahead (drops tickers using missing data from the future)
Flags prices.bfill() as filling gaps with future prices
Flags the momentum z-score normalised with full-sample mean/std
Flags rev.rank(pct=True) as ranking over the time axis (uses future rows)
Flags the centered rolling volatility window (center=True)
Flags the high-vol regime threshold taken from the full-sample quantile
Flags weekly momentum reindexed with method='bfill' (Friday's value used earlier in the week)
Flags fundamentals merged on period_end instead of filing date (reference time vs availability)
features_fixed.py runs on the sample data and passes the grader's perturbation and truncation leak checks
Does not report the cross-sectional cs_move feature (rank axis=1) as a leak
The report describes a dynamic check of the fix (perturbing or truncating data after t)

evals.prompt: We're about to put an LLM agent live on Binance USD-M perps (BTCUSDT and ETHUSDT). It runs in an OpenClaw-style setup: the LLM proposes trades through tool calls to a local executor, and we've installed two community skills from a marketplace for news sentiment and on-chain signals. Before it touches real money, write a design doc, risk_execution_design.md, for the execution/risk layer: which checks go where, concrete default numbers, what happens in high-volatility or low-margin conditions, and how we test that it actually holds up against bad or manipulated LLM output. Include a short Python sketch of the core check (save it as gate_sketch.py).
evals.expected_output: A design doc with a non-bypassable last-mile gate, regime/trust-conditioned budgets, cooldowns, allowlists, reduce-only states, audit logs and an adversarial test plan with attack-success and false-block metrics; plus a runnable sketch.
expectations: Puts a deterministic, non-bypassable gate between the LLM/strategy and the exchange executor
Treats LLM output and the marketplace skills as untrusted (prompt injection and supply-chain risk addressed)
Tightens limits based on trust signals (skill provenance, injection alerts or source reliability)
Clamps over-limit requests down to allowed size (partial approval), not only reject
Gives concrete leverage caps that tighten in high-volatility regimes
Gives concrete cooldown and order-rate limits
Gives a concrete slippage cap
Uses allowlists for tools/venues/symbols (e.g. only BTCUSDT/ETHUSDT, no withdrawals)
Defines a reduce-only state for low margin and/or extreme volatility or drawdown
Accounts for funding payments and/or maintenance-margin/liquidation mechanics
Logs an audit record per decision (rule hit, budgets/limits, state snapshot)
Test plan includes parameter escalation, order flooding/rapid flipping, and tool/venue misuse attacks
Test metrics include both attack success (leakage) and false blocks of legitimate orders
gate_sketch.py runs without errors

evals.prompt: Our team built a TradingAgents-style multi-agent LLM trading system on GPT-4o: four analyst agents, a bull/bear researcher debate, a trader agent, and an LLM risk manager that makes the final call. We backtested it on the current S&P 500 constituents from Jan 2023 to Dec 2024, trading at the close of the day each signal is generated, with no transaction costs. After trying about 40 prompt variants, the best one has an annualized Sharpe of about 2.2. returns.csv has the daily returns of that best variant and of an equal-weight buy-and-hold benchmark. My manager wants to present this to the investment committee next week. Is the result credible? Write review.md with your verdict, the specific problems, any numbers you compute from the data, and what we need to do before presenting.
evals.expected_output: Verdict: not credible as-is; flags survivorship, pretraining look-ahead, multiple testing (deflated Sharpe), same-close fills, no costs, terminal LLM risk manager; computes dependence-aware stats vs benchmark; gives a concrete remediation plan.
expectations: Gives a clear verdict that the result is not credible / not presentable as-is
Flags survivorship bias from using current S&P 500 constituents
Flags GPT-4o pretraining look-ahead for 2023-2024 and recommends post-cutoff or anonymised evaluation
Flags selection from ~40 prompt variants and computes or applies a deflated Sharpe ratio or equivalent correction
Flags execution at the signal-day close and recommends next-open/next-bar execution
Flags missing transaction costs and recommends a cost model with sensitivity
Computes performance statistics from returns.csv (e.g. Sharpe, drawdown)
Uses a dependence-aware or paired method for uncertainty (block bootstrap, HAC/Newey-West, or paired test vs benchmark)
Compares the strategy against the benchmark (excess return, alpha/beta, or difference test)
Flags the LLM risk manager as the final decision node and recommends a deterministic risk gate after it (jailbreak/injection risk)
Recommends a sealed out-of-sample or walk-forward holdout for prompt selection
